strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: existing visual reasoning methods specialize in either text-based or visually-grounded reasoning, and no single mode dominates across domains; the paper proposes a principled way to combine both.

Technically sound design: a unified sequence format with mode-prefix tokens enables joint SFT training of two reasoning modes, and AdaGRPO introduces a well-justified mode-relative advantage (derived via a Gaussian CDF over group reward statistics) plus prefix-guided exploration to address genuine failure modes of vanilla GRPO (mode collapse, lack of explicit mode-level credit assignment).

Extensive empirical evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, general perception, hallucination, spatial reasoning) and two model scales (3B/7B), with numerous strong and recent baselines (both text-based and visually-grounded specialized models), showing consistent improvements over the base model where single-mode baselines fail on some benchmarks.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each AdaGRPO component (Ada-Adv, PG-Exp), the necessity of mode-specific prefixes vs. naive data mixing, the value of curriculum learning, and a dedicated experiment showing that SFT alone cannot learn effective mode selection (motivating the RL stage).

Insightful analysis of training dynamics (reward curves per mode/task) and fine-grained mode-selection statistics (e.g., Figure 4, 5) that support the claimed mechanism, along with an 'upper bound' analysis showing headroom and complementarity between modes.

Good reproducibility: detailed prompts, data construction pipeline, and hyperparameters are provided in the appendix; extensive qualitative case studies illustrate concrete strengths/weaknesses of each mode.
weaknesses: The framework is only instantiated and validated with exactly two reasoning modes (text-based and box-grounded); claims about general extensibility to more modes (Appendix B.4) remain purely speculative/future work without empirical support.

There remains a substantial gap between AdaVaR and the reported 'upper bound' of adaptive reasoning (e.g., 50.8 vs 56.8 average for the 3B model), indicating mode-selection capability, while improved over SFT, is still far from optimal — this tempers the significance of the central claimed contribution (context-adaptive selection).

All experiments are built on a single backbone family (Qwen2.5-VL), so generalization of the method (and especially of AdaGRPO's Gaussian-based mode-relative advantage, which relies on distributional assumptions about small-sample reward groups) to other LVLM backbones or larger scales is untested.

The training pipeline is fairly complex and involves multiple curated/filtered datasets, task-specific curriculum stages, and a heuristic offline mode-switching mechanism at inference time, which may hurt reproducibility and generality despite the detailed documentation.

Some baseline results are self-reproduced (marked with *), and no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for the main results, making it harder to assess the robustness/significance of the reported gains, some of which (e.g., MathVision, MathVerse for 7B) are smaller than for specialized single-mode competitors.

The core novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior GRPO-style RL for reasoning: the mode-prefix mechanism and mode-relative advantage are reasonable but relatively straightforward extensions of existing group-relative RL formulations rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: unifying complementary text-based and visually-grounded reasoning modes into a single adaptive model rather than specializing in one domain.

Technically sound extension of GRPO (AdaGRPO) with three clearly motivated components (prefix-guided exploration, mode-relative advantage via Gaussian CDF estimation, curriculum data scheduling), each individually ablated in Table 3.

Extensive empirical validation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, spatial, hallucination, general) and two model scales (3B/7B), with AdaVaR-7B surpassing GPT-4o on average and consistently beating the Qwen2.5-VL baseline on every benchmark, unlike compared single-mode methods.

Thorough analysis section: mode-selection behavior across fine-grained categories, attention visualization justifying mode choice, error decomposition into selection vs. reasoning errors, comparison against naive ensemble baselines (Expert Pick, Max(GRD,TXT)) showing the learned policy is genuinely better than heuristic routing.

Strong reproducibility effort: detailed prompts, data construction pipeline, hyperparameters, and an SFT-only ablation (Appendix C.2) that convincingly shows mode selection cannot be reliably learned without the online RL stage.
Efficiency analysis (theoretical FLOPs and wall-clock time) shows AdaGRPO adds negligible overhead over vanilla GRPO by sharing KV cache across mode prefixes.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is an incremental extension of GRPO (adding token-position-specific advantages and a Gaussian-CDF-based pairwise preference term); the Gaussian independence assumption used to derive mode-relative advantage is not itself validated against alternative estimators.

On several individual benchmarks (e.g., MathVision, MathVerse) specialist text-based models like OVR-7B substantially outperform AdaVaR-7B, so the 'general' model's aggregate gain partly reflects averaging rather than uniformly strong performance; the equal-weighting average schema across benchmarks of very different sizes/difficulties is not well justified.
Many baseline numbers are self-reproduced (marked with *) rather than taken from original papers, which could introduce evaluation inconsistencies or unintentional advantages for the proposed method.

The reasoning-mode taxonomy is limited to only two modes in the main experiments; while width/depth extensions are discussed in the appendix, no actual experiments demonstrate scalability beyond two modes, leaving the generality of the MoVT paradigm partly speculative.

Data construction relies on a fairly complex, multi-stage pipeline (distillation from Orsta, GPT-4o/Qwen-72B based filtering and re-formatting) whose quality is validated only via small-scale spot checks (100 samples), raising some concern about label/data noise propagating into training.

No variance/multiple-seed results are reported for the RL training, which is known to be sensitive to random seeds and rollout sampling, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a reasonable and practically relevant problem: existing visual reasoning models specialize in either text-based (math-oriented) or visually-grounded (perception-oriented) reasoning, and no single mode dominates across domains.

The experimental protocol is broad: 8 diverse benchmarks spanning math, spatial reasoning, hallucination, and general perception are used, with many single-mode baselines reproduced for fair comparison.

Extensive ablation studies are provided (prefix-guided exploration, adaptive advantage, curriculum data ordering, SFT data ratio, prompt sensitivity, robustness to image noise), along with computational efficiency analysis and qualitative case studies, showing considerable engineering effort.

The paper includes thoughtful auxiliary analyses (attention visualization for mode selection, fine-grained mode-selection statistics, error decomposition into selection vs. reasoning errors) that attempt to explain the mechanism behind the proposed method rather than just reporting end metrics.
Reasonable reproducibility documentation (hyperparameters, prompts, data construction pipeline) is provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim—that a general model must adaptively mix modes because no single mode dominates—is significantly undercut by the paper's own Table 1: OVR-7B, a single text-based reasoning model, achieves essentially the same average accuracy as AdaVaR-7B (55.76 vs. 55.82) and substantially outperforms AdaVaR-7B on MathVision (46.4 vs. 28.5) and MathVerse (54.6 vs. 43.0). This directly contradicts the paper's premise and is not adequately discussed or reconciled.

The gap between AdaVaR's achieved performance and the reported 'upper bound' of adaptive reasoning (50.8 vs. 56.8 for the 3B model) is large, indicating that the learned mode-selection policy is still far from optimal and that a substantial fraction of the paper's claimed benefit is aspirational rather than realized.

Ablations show that the key novel component (adaptive/mode-relative advantage in AdaGRPO) contributes only a small improvement (50.3 to 50.8 average accuracy), suggesting the core algorithmic novelty has limited empirical impact relative to more standard components (prefix-guided exploration, curriculum data).

The technical contribution is largely a combination of existing ideas (prefix-conditioned generation, group-relative advantage estimation via Gaussian CDF, curriculum learning, DeepSeek-R1-style rule-based rewards) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the 'mode-relative advantage' is a fairly simple two-group comparison.

Only two reasoning modes (text-based and bounding-box grounded) are studied experimentally; the appendix's discussion of 'width/depth extension' to more modes is purely conceptual with no experiments, making the 'general visual reasoning' framing somewhat oversold relative to what is empirically demonstrated.

Selection errors still constitute a non-trivial share of total errors (up to about 25% on some datasets, e.g., POPE), and mode selection error patterns (Tables 9-10) show the model still struggles even in domains where one mode has a clear advantage, questioning how robust the adaptive selection mechanism really is.

Models are only evaluated at 3B/7B scale; there is no evidence the method scales to larger backbones or generalizes beyond the specific bounding-box grounding format and math/perception benchmark suite used.
The reward design and RL objective largely mirror DeepSeek-R1-style rule-based accuracy/format rewards, limiting algorithmic novelty beyond the advantage decomposition.

strengths: Clearly motivated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates (via Fig 1b and Table 1) that existing text-based and visually-grounded reasoning models each excel in different domains but fail to generalize, motivating the need for an adaptive/general reasoning paradigm.

Principled technical contribution: AdaGRPO introduces prefix-guided mode exploration and a mathematically grounded mode-relative advantage (via Gaussian CDF comparison of reward distributions) that explicitly addresses the under-exploration and lack of mode-preference modeling issues in vanilla GRPO.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks (math, hallucination, visual search, spatial reasoning, general perception) with many strong single-mode baselines (text-based and visually-grounded), showing AdaVaR is the only model family that improves over the base model across all datasets.

Extensive and rigorous ablation/analysis suite: mode-ratio sensitivity in SFT, necessity of mode-specific prefixes, curriculum data ordering, prefix format sensitivity, system-prompt sensitivity, upper-bound analysis, attention visualization for mode selection, error decomposition (selection vs. reasoning errors), and computational efficiency comparisons (GRPO vs AdaGRPO, inference cost).

Good qualitative case studies across multiple benchmarks illustrating interpretable differences in reasoning patterns between modes and reasonable context-dependent mode selection by the trained model.

Thoughtful discussion of scalability (width/depth extension to more modes) and limitations (multilingual, other modalities), indicating awareness of the broader research trajectory even if not fully implemented.
weaknesses: Performance gains, while consistent, are often modest and on several individual benchmarks specialized single-mode models (e.g., OVR-7B on MathVision/MathVerse/WeMath, DeepEyes on POPE/V*) still outperform AdaVaR-7B, tempering the 'general reasoning' claim somewhat.

The large remaining gap between AdaVaR and the oracle upper bound (e.g., 50.8 vs 56.8 average accuracy for the 3B model) shows mode-selection capability is still far from optimal, which is acknowledged but not fully addressed.

The RL and SFT data construction pipeline is quite complex and involves multiple filtering/distillation/annotation steps (using GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, difficulty filtering, curriculum splitting), which may hinder exact reproducibility despite detailed appendix documentation.

Only two reasoning modes (text-based and visually-grounded) are empirically validated; the proposed width/depth extensions to more modes are purely conceptual/discussion without experiments, leaving open whether the approach truly scales as claimed.

The inference-time mode-switching heuristic (retrying with the other mode upon repetitive/stuck generation) is a practical but somewhat ad hoc addition whose isolated contribution to the reported numbers is not clearly quantified or ablated.

The core algorithmic novelty is an incremental (though well-motivated) extension of GRPO for mode-aware exploration and advantage assignment, rather than a fundamentally new RL paradigm; similar dual-branch/preference-based advantage ideas exist in adjacent RL literature.

Comparisons rely on officially released checkpoints re-evaluated by the authors for missing benchmarks rather than a fully unified retraining/evaluation protocol, which, although reasonable practice, introduces potential inconsistencies in evaluation settings across compared models.
